nameStory: Blue water-speedwell gets its name from its preference for wet places and its tiny blue flowers that seem to speed by in the current of streams and pond edges. The 'speedwell' part comes from an old tradition of giving these flowers to travelers as a good luck charm for a speedy, safe journey. The 'water' part is obvious once you see where this little plant loves to grow!
description: Blue water-speedwell is a small, low-growing aquatic plant that hugs the muddy edges of ponds, streams, and wetlands. It spreads along the ground or floats partially submerged, rarely getting taller than a few inches. This delicate plant produces tiny four-petaled blue flowers that peek up from among small, oval leaves. It's easily overlooked unless you're looking closely at the water's edge.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny blue flowers with four rounded petals, each about the size of a pencil eraser, growing singly from where leaves meet the stem. The petals feel papery-thin and have a subtle sweet scent.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves arranged in pairs directly across from each other on the stem. They feel smooth and slightly fleshy, like tiny lettuce leaves, and have very faint teeth along the edges.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Creeps along muddy shores or floats partially submerged in shallow water, forming loose mats. Stems feel soft and squishy, easily bent without breaking.

idTips.label: Habitat Clue
idTips.description: Always found with its roots in mud or shallow water - never in dry soil. Look for it where your shoes would get wet if you stepped closer to the water.

habitat: Blue water-speedwell thrives in the muddy margins of ponds, slow-moving streams, and shallow wetlands throughout New England. You'll find it in places where the soil stays consistently moist or waterlogged, often growing alongside cattails, arrowhead, and other water-loving plants. It prefers sunny to partly shady spots where it can get good light while keeping its feet wet.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as water warms, with fresh green shoots appearing in late spring. Early flowers may start blooming in May in warmer locations.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with tiny blue flowers appearing continuously from June through August. This is the best time to spot and identify the plant when flowers are most abundant.
seasonality.fall: Flowering continues into early fall, though less prolifically. Plants begin to die back as temperatures drop, turning brownish.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely in most areas, surviving as roots in the mud. In mild winters or protected spots, some evergreen growth may persist underwater.

funFact: Blue water-speedwell can actually live completely underwater for weeks during floods, continuing to photosynthesize while submerged - it's like a tiny aquatic shapeshifter that seamlessly transitions between being a land plant and a water plant!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small blue-flowered speedwells, but blue water-speedwell is the only one that grows directly in water or wet mud. If your feet aren't getting wet, you're probably looking at a different speedwell species. Remember: blue water-speedwell needs wet feet!
contextualKnowledge: The speedwell genus includes many species that can be tricky to tell apart, but habitat is your best friend - each species has very specific preferences for soil moisture and growing conditions. Don't worry about memorizing all the speedwell species; focus on where you find them and you'll narrow down the possibilities quickly.
compareHints: Among New England's many speedwells, blue water-speedwell is unique in its aquatic lifestyle - while American brooklime also likes wet areas, it grows taller and has larger flowers. Marsh speedwell prefers similar wet habitats but has much narrower, lance-shaped leaves instead of the oval leaves of blue water-speedwell. Most other speedwells prefer drier soils and won't be found with their roots in standing water.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's speedwells, heath speedwell is unique for its distinctly creeping, mat-forming growth habit and very fuzzy stems and leaves.
Among New England's speedwells, thyme-leaved speedwell is unique in its strongly creeping, mat-forming habit - most other speedwells grow more upright.
Among the speedwells, germander speedwell stands out for having the brightest blue flowers and the most prominent flower stalks that clearly rise above the foliage.
Among the speedwells, corn speedwell is distinguished by its fuzzy leaves and very small size - it's one of the tiniest in the genus.
Among the speedwells, marsh speedwell is distinctive for its wetland habitat and very narrow leaves.
Bird's-eye speedwell stands out from its many speedwell relatives by having the brightest, most intensely blue flowers with the most prominent dark radiating lines.
Among the many speedwells in New England, American brooklime is the water-lover of the group.
Among New England's many speedwell species, purslane speedwell stands out for its highly variable leaf shapes on a single plant and its preference for the most disturbed habitats.
Unlike the upright thyme-leaved speedwell or the larger-flowered Germander speedwell, slender speedwell stays flat to the ground with its characteristic thread-thin stems.

Long-leaved Speedwell towers over most other New England speedwells - while species like Thyme-leaved Speedwell hug the ground and Germander Speedwell stays low in lawns, this species stands tall with substantial flower spikes.
Unlike most other New England speedwells that are annual weeds or die back completely in winter, creeping speedwell is a true perennial that forms permanent mats.

Among New England speedwells, broadleaf speedwell stands out for its relatively large, oval leaves and dense flower spikes - most other speedwells have much smaller, narrower leaves and more open flower arrangements.
Among New England's speedwells, ivy-leaved speedwell is easily distinguished by its distinctive lobed leaves that look like tiny ivy leaves.
Unlike its lowland speedwell relatives that grow in fields and gardens, American alpine speedwell is the mountain specialist of the family.
Spiked speedwell towers over its New England speedwell relatives, most of which are small, creeping, or prostrate plants with much smaller flower clusters.
Among the many speedwells in New England, Pink Ivy-leaved Speedwell stands out for its distinctly lobed, ivy-like leaves - most other speedwells have simple, unlobed leaves.
Grey field-speedwell stands out from its speedwell relatives primarily by its grayish leaf color and extremely small size.
Among the speedwells, chain speedwell is unique for its strong preference for aquatic habitats and its creeping, often floating growth habit.
